summary: This assessment unit details the processes of land degradation, its drivers, and the challenges in attributing these changes to climate change versus human management. It highlights the role of climate change as a threat multiplier for land degradation, particularly through intensified rainfall, warming, and altered precipitation regimes, while noting that land management remains a critical factor in controlling degradation rates.

heading_path: 4.2.1.2 Land degradation processes and climate change
passages.text: Among land degradation processes, those responding more directly to climate change pressures include all types of erosion and SOM declines (soil focus), salinisation, sodification and permafrost thawing (soil/water focus), waterlogging of dry ecosystems and drying of wet ecosystems (water focus), and a broad group of biologically-mediated processes like woody encroachment, biological invasions, pest outbreaks (biotic focus), together with biological soil crust destruction and increased burning (soil/biota focus).

heading_path: 4.2.1.2 Land degradation processes and climate change
passages.text: Important exceptions are three processes in which climate change is a dominant global or regional pressure and the main driver of their current acceleration. These are: coastal erosion as affected by sea level rise and increased storm frequency/intensity (high agreement, medium evidence); permafrost thawing responding to warming (high agreement, robust evidence); and increased burning responding to warming and altered precipitation regimes (high agreement, robust evidence).
passages.topic: Climate change drivers of land degradation

passages.text: Studies suggest that erosion rates of conventionally tilled agricultural fields exceed the rate at which soil is generated by one to two orders of magnitude.

The most important direct impacts of climate change on land degradation are the results of increasing temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and intensification of rainfall. These changes will, in various combinations, cause changes in erosion rates and the processes driving both increases and decreases of soil erosion.

Rainfall intensity is a key climatic driver of soil erosion. Early modelling studies and theory suggest that light rainfall events will decrease while heavy rainfall events increase at about 7% per degree of warming. Such changes result in increased intensity of rainfall, which increases the erosive power of rainfall (erosivity) and hence enhances the likelihood of water erosion.

In summary, rainfall changes attributed to human-induced climate change have already intensified drivers of land degradation (robust evidence, high agreement) but attributing land degradation to climate change is challenging because of the importance of land management (medium evidence, high agreement).

An assessment of the global severity of soil erosion in agriculture, based on 1673 measurements around the world (compiled from 201 peer-reviewed articles), indicated that the global net median rate of soil formation (i.e., formation minus erosion) is about 0.004 mm yr–1 (about 0.05 t ha–1 yr–1) compared with the median net rate of soil loss in agricultural fields, 1.52 mm yr–1 (about 18 t ha–1 yr–1) in tilled fields and 0.065 mm yr–1 (about 0.8 t ha–1 yr–1) in no-till fields. This means that the rate of soil erosion from agricultural fields is between 380 (conventional tilling) and 16 times (no-till) the natural rate of soil formation (medium agreement, limited evidence).

Soils contain about 1500 Gt of organic carbon, which is about 1.8 times more carbon than in the atmosphere and 2.3–3.3 times more than what is held in the terrestrial vegetation of the world. Hence, land degradation, including land conversion leading to soil carbon losses, has the potential to impact on the atmospheric concentration of CO2 substantially.
